claim: QFL T cells are present at a frequency of ~1 in 1000 of the siIEL CD8+ T cells in naïve WT mice.
source: QFL T cells were present at a frequency of ~1 in 1000 of the siIEL CD8+ T cells, which was 10 times more frequent than in the spleen (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1b and c, which displays frequencies of QFL-Dex+ cells in siIEL compartment.

claim: QFL T cells are present at a frequency 10 times higher in siIEL than in the spleen of naïve WT mice.
source: QFL T cells were present at a frequency of ~1 in 1000 of the siIEL CD8+ T cells, which was 10 times more frequent than in the spleen (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: Supported by quantitative flow cytometry data comparing frequencies between spleen and siIEL compartments shown in Figure 1b and c.

claim: The average number of QFL T cells in the siIEL compartment of naïve WT mice is comparable to the population in the spleen.
source: The average number of QFL T cells – defined as CD45+CD19-TCRβ+CD4-QFL-Dex-PE+APC+ (Figure 1a) – detected in the siIEL compartment of naïve WT mice was comparable to the population in the spleen.
evidence: Supported by absolute cell counts shown in Figure 1b and c comparing spleen and siIEL compartments.

claim: Approximately 80% of splenic QFL T cells express the invariant TCR Vα segment Vα3.2.
source: Consistent with prior studies, ~80% of the splenic QFL T cells expressed the 'invariant' TCR Vα segment Vα3.2 which was significantly higher than the proportion of Vα3.2-expressing cells within the total CD8+ T population in the spleen (<5%) (Figure 1d and e; Guan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1d and e showing Vα3.2 expression, and cited prior work (Guan et al., 2017).

claim: Less than 5% of total CD8+ T cells in the spleen express Vα3.2.
source: Consistent with prior studies, ~80% of the splenic QFL T cells expressed the 'invariant' TCR Vα segment Vα3.2 which was significantly higher than the proportion of Vα3.2-expressing cells within the total CD8+ T population in the spleen (<5%) (Figure 1d and e; Guan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1d and e comparing Vα3.2 expression in QFL T cells versus total CD8+ T cells.

claim: QFL T cells in the siIEL compartment contain a relatively larger proportion of Vα3.2+ cells (20.1%) compared to total CD8+ TCRαβ siIELs (<10%).
source: Notably, QFL T cells in the siIEL compartment also contained a relatively larger proportion of Vα3.2+ cells (20.1%) compared to the total CD8+ TCRαβ siIELs (<10%) (Figure 1f and g).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1f and g showing Vα3.2 expression frequencies in siIEL QFL T cells versus total siIEL CD8+ T cells.

claim: The average percentage of Vα3.2+ cells within the QFL T population is lower in the siIEL compartment (20.1%) than in the spleen (63.3%).
source: The average percentage of Vα3.2+ cells within the QFL T population (20.1%) was lower in the siIEL compartment than in the spleen (63.3%).
evidence: Supported by comparison of flow cytometry data from spleen and siIEL compartments.

claim: Splenic and siIEL QFL T cells are essentially all CD8+ T cells, as they are barely detectable within the CD4+ T population.
source: Both the splenic and siIEL QFL T cells were essentially all CD8+ T cells, as these cells were barely detectable within the CD4+ T population (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing minimal CD4+ QFL T cells.

claim: QFL-Dex shows improved sensitivity and specificity for QFL T cell detection compared to QFL-Tet.
source: Moreover, in comparison with QFL-Tet, QFL-Dex showed improved sensitivity and specificity for QFL T cell detection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by comparative flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing detection differences between QFL-Tet and QFL-Dex.

claim: Vα3.2+QFL T cells contain a significantly larger proportion of CD44hi cells (~90%) than Vα3.2-QFL T cells.
source: We observed that Vα3.2+QFL T cells contained a significantly larger proportion of CD44hi cells (~90%) than the Vα3.2-QFL T cells, suggesting that the antigen-experienced phenotype of the QFL T population was mainly contributed by the Vα3.2-expressing subpopulation (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2a and b showing CD44 expression on Vα3.2+ versus Vα3.2- QFL T cells.

claim: The antigen-experienced phenotype of the QFL T population is mainly contributed by the Vα3.2-expressing subpopulation.
source: We observed that Vα3.2+QFL T cells contained a significantly larger proportion of CD44hi cells (~90%) than the Vα3.2-QFL T cells, suggesting that the antigen-experienced phenotype of the QFL T population was mainly contributed by the Vα3.2-expressing subpopulation (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Vα3.2+ QFL T cells have ~90% CD44hi cells while Vα3.2- cells have lower percentages, shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: Only around 20% of the total Vα3.2+CD8+ T population express high CD44.
source: In contrast, only around 20% of the total Vα3.2+CD8+ T population expressed high CD44.
evidence: Stated as a comparison to the Vα3.2+ QFL T cells, based on flow cytometry analysis.

claim: The percentage of CD44hi cells within the total Vα3.2+CD8+ T population is slightly higher compared to the Vα3.2- population.
source: It is worth noting that the percentage of CD44hi cells within the total Vα3.2+CD8+ T population was slightly higher compared to the Vα3.2- population (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), which was in line with a previous report (Prasad et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and cited prior work (Prasad et al., 2021).

claim: A relatively larger fraction of Vα3.2+QFL T cells lack CD4 and CD8αβ expression but express CD8αα compared to the Vα3.2- subpopulation in the siIEL compartment.
source: A relatively larger fraction of Vα3.2+QFL T cells lacked CD4 and CD8αβ expression but expressed CD8αα compared to the Vα3.2- subpopulation suggesting that the majority of Vα3.2+ QFL T cells were CD8αα+ natIELs (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2c and d showing CD8α and CD8β expression patterns.

claim: The majority of Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in the siIEL compartment are CD8αα+ natIELs.
source: A relatively larger fraction of Vα3.2+QFL T cells lacked CD4 and CD8αβ expression but expressed CD8αα compared to the Vα3.2- subpopulation suggesting that the majority of Vα3.2+ QFL T cells were CD8αα+ natIELs (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Vα3.2+ QFL T cells predominantly express CD8αα, a hallmark of natIELs, shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: No difference in CD8αα expression was observed between the total Vα3.2+ and Vα3.2- CD8+ IEL populations.
source: No such difference was observed between the total Vα3.2+ and Vα3.2- CD8+ IEL populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b comparing CD8αα expression in total Vα3.2+ versus Vα3.2- IEL populations.

claim: Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in both the spleen and siIEL compartment are unconventional CD8+ T cells likely derived from the same precursors in the thymus.
source: These observations indicate that the Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in both the spleen and siIEL compartment are unconventional CD8+ T cells which likely are derived from the same precursors in the thymus.
evidence: Inferred from the shared unconventional phenotypes (CD44hi in spleen, CD8αα+ in siIEL) of Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in both tissues.

claim: TAP is required for the presence of both splenic and siIEL Vα3.2+QFL T cells.
source: While we consistently observed loss of both the splenic and siIEL Vα3.2+QFL T cells in TAP-KO mice, the populations were detectable in both tissues of Qa-1b-KO or ERAP1-KO mice with a slightly reduced population size in the spleen of Qa-1b-KO mice (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3a showing absence of Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in TAP-KO mice.

claim: Vα3.2+ QFL T populations are detectable in both spleen and siIEL of Qa-1b-KO or ERAP1-KO mice.
source: While we consistently observed loss of both the splenic and siIEL Vα3.2+QFL T cells in TAP-KO mice, the populations were detectable in both tissues of Qa-1b-KO or ERAP1-KO mice with a slightly reduced population size in the spleen of Qa-1b-KO mice (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3a showing presence of Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in Qa-1b-KO and ERAP1-KO mice.

claim: The phenotype of splenic Vα3.2- QFL T cells is not significantly affected by Qa-1b or ERAP1 deficiency.
source: In contrast, the phenotype of splenic Vα3.2- QFL T cells was not significantly affected (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3b and c showing no significant change in CD44 expression in Vα3.2- QFL T cells in knockout mice.

claim: siIEL Vα3.2+ QFL T cells show almost complete loss of the unconventional natIEL phenotype including CD8αα expression in Qa-1b-KO mice.
source: Similar pattern of phenotype change was observed for the siIEL Vα3.2+ QFL T cells which showed almost complete loss of the unconventional natIEL phenotype including CD8αα expression in Qa-1b-KO mice (Figure 3d and e, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3d and e and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing loss of CD8αα expression in Qa-1b-KO mice.

claim: TAP is required for the presence of the Vα3.2+ QFL T population.
source: These results demonstrate that TAP and Qa-1b both play a role in the establishment of the unconventional Vα3.2+ QFL T population, with TAP being required for the presence of the population, and Qa-1b being required for the unconventional phenotype imprinting of these cells.
evidence: Supported by data showing absence of Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in TAP-KO mice (Figure 3a).

claim: Qa-1b is required for the unconventional phenotype imprinting of Vα3.2+ QFL T cells.
source: These results demonstrate that TAP and Qa-1b both play a role in the establishment of the unconventional Vα3.2+ QFL T population, with TAP being required for the presence of the population, and Qa-1b being required for the unconventional phenotype imprinting of these cells.
evidence: Supported by data showing loss of unconventional phenotype (CD44hi, CD8αα+) in Qa-1b-KO mice while cells are still present (Figure 3b-e).

claim: Total splenic Vα3.2+CD8αβ+ T cells show a similar loss of memory phenotype in Qa-1b-KO and ERAP1-KO mice.
source: It is also worth noting that total splenic Vα3.2+CD8αβ+ T cells showed a similar loss of memory phenotype in Qa-1b-KO and ERAP1-KO mice, whereas Vα3.2-CD8αβ+T cells did not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c showing CD44 expression in total Vα3.2+ versus Vα3.2- CD8+ T cells in knockout mice.

claim: Vα3.2-CD8αβ+T cells do not show loss of memory phenotype in Qa-1b-KO and ERAP1-KO mice.
source: It is also worth noting that total splenic Vα3.2+CD8αβ+ T cells showed a similar loss of memory phenotype in Qa-1b-KO and ERAP1-KO mice, whereas Vα3.2-CD8αβ+T cells did not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c showing no change in CD44 expression in Vα3.2- CD8+ T cells in knockout mice.

claim: QFLTg cells recapitulate the unconventional phenotype of polyclonal Vα3.2+QFL T cells with high CD44 expression in the spleen and CD8αα expression in the siIEL compartment.
source: Phenotypically, the QFLTg cells recapitulated the unconventional phenotype of polyclonal Vα3.2+QFL T cells with high CD44 expression in the spleen and CD8αα expression in the siIEL compartment.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c showing CD44 and CD8αα expression in QFLTg cells.

claim: OT-1 cells are phenotypically similar to conventional naïve CD8+ T cells, expressing low to intermediate levels of CD44 in the spleen and lacking CD8αα expression in the gut.
source: In contrast, OT-1 cells were phenotypically similar to conventional naïve CD8+ T cells, as they expressed low to intermediate levels of CD44 in the spleen and lacked CD8αα expression in the gut (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b, c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c showing CD44 and CD8αα expression in OT-1 cells.

claim: Splenic QFLTg cells are significantly more responsive to IL-15 or IL-7/IL-18 stimulation than OT-1 cells.
source: In keeping with their virtual memory surface marker phenotype, splenic QFLTg cells were significantly more responsive to IL-15 or IL-7/IL-18 stimulation than OT-1 cells (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 4a showing CTV dilution in response to cytokine stimulation.

claim: At 72 hr, ~80% of splenic QFLTg cells had proliferated in response to cytokines, compared with only ~50% of OT-1 cells.
source: At 72 hr, ~80% of QFLTg cells had proliferated in response to the cytokines, compared with only ~50% of OT-1 cells (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by quantitative proliferation data in Figure 4b showing percentages of proliferated cells.

claim: Both QFLTg and OT-1 cells from siIEL are less responsive to IL-15 than the splenic population.
source: In contrast, T cells isolated from the siIEL compartment of QFLTg or OT-1 mice showed a distinct pattern of cytokine responsiveness from the splenic T cells. First, both QFLTg and OT-1 cells from siIEL were less responsive to IL-15 than the splenic population.
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 4c and d comparing siIEL and splenic responses to IL-15.

claim: siIEL QFLTg cells show significantly reduced proliferation in response to cytokines, especially to the combination of IL-7/IL-18, compared with OT-1 cells.
source: Second, siIEL QFLTg cells showed significantly reduced proliferation in response to the cytokines, especially to the combination of IL-7/IL-18, as compared with OT-1 cells (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 4c and d showing reduced CTV dilution in siIEL QFLTg cells compared to OT-1 cells.

claim: A large fraction (~60%) of splenic QFLTg cells express high levels of IFN-ɣ after 4.5 hr stimulation with FL9 peptide.
source: A large fraction (~60%) of splenic QFLTg cells expressed high levels of IFN-ɣ under these conditions, while only 6% of OT-1 cells did so (Figure 4g and h).
evidence: Supported by intracellular cytokine staining data in Figure 4g and h showing IFN-ɣ production after peptide stimulation.

claim: Only 6% of splenic OT-1 cells express high levels of IFN-ɣ after 4.5 hr stimulation with SL8 peptide.
source: A large fraction (~60%) of splenic QFLTg cells expressed high levels of IFN-ɣ under these conditions, while only 6% of OT-1 cells did so (Figure 4g and h).
evidence: Supported by intracellular cytokine staining data in Figure 4g and h showing IFN-ɣ production after peptide stimulation.

claim: siIEL QFLTg cells show relatively higher basal levels of IFN-ɣ expression than OT-1 cells.
source: Notably, despite the low responsiveness to epitopes, siIEL QFLTg cells showed relatively higher basal levels of IFN-ɣ expression than OT-1 cells (Figure 4i and j).
evidence: Supported by intracellular cytokine staining data in Figure 4i and j showing basal IFN-ɣ levels without peptide stimulation.

claim: Neither QFLTg nor OT-1 cells from the siIEL compartment show significant IFN-ɣ production at 4.5 hr after peptide stimulation.
source: In contrast to the hyperresponsiveness of splenic QFLTg cells to their ligand, neither QFLTg nor OT-1 cells from the siIEL compartment showed significant IFN-ɣ production at 4.5 hr.
evidence: Supported by intracellular cytokine staining data in Figure 4i and j showing minimal IFN-ɣ production in siIEL cells after peptide stimulation.

claim: Vα3.2+QFL T cells in the spleen are functionally innate-like.
source: We conclude that Vα3.2+QFL T cells in the spleen are functionally innate-like, whereas the population with the same TCR specificity in the small intestine shows functional features of natIEL.
evidence: Inferred from data showing rapid cytokine responsiveness and IFN-ɣ production by splenic QFLTg cells (Figure 4a, b, g, h).

claim: The Vα3.2+QFL T population in the small intestine shows functional features of natIEL.
source: We conclude that Vα3.2+QFL T cells in the spleen are functionally innate-like, whereas the population with the same TCR specificity in the small intestine shows functional features of natIEL.
evidence: Inferred from data showing reduced responsiveness to cytokines and peptides by siIEL QFLTg cells (Figure 4c, d, i, j).

claim: The absolute number of QFL T cells in the spleen is unaffected by the absence of gut microbiota in either young or old mice.
source: First, we found the absolute number of QFL T cells in the spleen was unaffected by the absence of gut microbiota in either young or old mice.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5a and b comparing splenic QFL T cell numbers in SPF versus GF mice.

claim: The frequency of QFL T cells in the spleen is relatively higher in GF than in SPF mice, as a result of a decreased number of non-QFL CD8+ T cells in the spleen of GF mice.
source: The frequency of QFL T cells was relatively higher in GF than in SPF mice, as a result of a decreased number of non-QFL CD8+ T cells in the spleen of GF mice (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5a and b showing frequencies of QFL T cells in SPF versus GF mice.

claim: The number and frequency of QFL T cells in siIEL compartment show no significant difference between GF and SPF mice of relatively young age (8~17 week).
source: Second, while the number and frequency of QFL T cells in siIEL compartment showed no significant difference between GF and SPF mice of relatively young age (8~17 week), the population was gradually lost in old GF mice (18~22 week) (Figure 5c and d)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5c and d comparing siIEL QFL T cells in young SPF versus GF mice.

claim: The QFL T cell population in the siIEL compartment is gradually lost in old GF mice (18~22 week).
source: Second, while the number and frequency of QFL T cells in siIEL compartment showed no significant difference between GF and SPF mice of relatively young age (8~17 week), the population was gradually lost in old GF mice (18~22 week) (Figure 5c and d)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5c and d showing decreased siIEL QFL T cells in old GF mice.

claim: The decrease in siIEL QFL T cells in GF mice starts from around 16 weeks of age.
source: with the decrease in GF mice starting from around 16 weeks of age (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as an observation from unpublished data.

claim: QFL T cells detected in the spleen or siIEL compartment of young SPF or GF mice show similar expressions of Vα3.2, CD44, and CD8αα.
source: In addition, the QFL T cells detected in the spleen or siIEL compartment of young SPF or GF mice showed similar expressions of Vα3.2, CD44, and CD8αα (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 comparing phenotypes in SPF versus GF mice.

claim: QFL T cells can home to the gut in the absence of microbiota.
source: We conclude that although QFL T cells could be home to the gut in the absence of microbiota, microbe-derived antigens or signals are required for their maintenance there.
evidence: Inferred from data showing presence of QFL T cells in young GF mice (Figure 5c and d).

claim: Microbe-derived antigens or signals are required for maintenance of QFL T cells in the gut.
source: We conclude that although QFL T cells could be home to the gut in the absence of microbiota, microbe-derived antigens or signals are required for their maintenance there.
evidence: Inferred from data showing loss of QFL T cells in old GF mice (Figure 5c and d).

claim: The average percentage of CD8αα+ cells among the total TCRβ+CD4- T population is proportionally larger in GF mice than SPF mice regardless of Vα3.2 expression.
source: Additionally, we observed that the average percentage of CD8αα+ cells among the total TCRβ+CD4- T population was proportionally larger in GF mice than SPF mice regardless of Vα3.2 expression, although the Vα3.2- population showed a more significant increase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b comparing CD8αα expression in SPF versus GF mice.

claim: Qa-1b restricted T cells can home to the small intestine epithelium and display a natIEL phenotype independent of gut microbiota.
source: Nevertheless, here we showed that Qa-1b restricted T cells could home to the small intestine epithelium and display a natIEL phenotype independent of gut microbiota.
evidence: Inferred from data showing presence of QFL T cells with natIEL phenotype in young GF mice (Figure 5c, d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Replacement of the P4 glutamic acid in FL9 peptide leads to complete loss of BEko8Z response.
source: By measuring the LacZ production of BEko8Z cells in response to Qa-1b-expressing Lmtk- (L-Qa-1b) cells pulsed with FYAAATPML (FL9-P4A) or FYAEAAPML (FL9-P6A), we found that in agreement with the prediction, replacement of the P6 threonine reduced TCR recognition, while replacement of the P4 glutamic acid led to the complete loss of the BEko8Z response (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by hybridoma assay data in Figure 6c showing loss of LacZ response with FL9-P4A peptide.

claim: Replacement of the P6 threonine in FL9 peptide reduces TCR recognition.
source: By measuring the LacZ production of BEko8Z cells in response to Qa-1b-expressing Lmtk- (L-Qa-1b) cells pulsed with FYAAATPML (FL9-P4A) or FYAEAAPML (FL9-P6A), we found that in agreement with the prediction, replacement of the P6 threonine reduced TCR recognition, while replacement of the P4 glutamic acid led to the complete loss of the BEko8Z response (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by hybridoma assay data in Figure 6c showing reduced LacZ response with FL9-P6A peptide.

claim: FYAEDGTPIL (FL10) is a peptide expressed in P. pentosaceus that cross-activates QFL T cells.
source: By measuring LacZ production of BEko8Z cells in response to L-Qa-1b cells pulsed with 50 nM of each candidate peptide, we identified a single stimulatory peptide FYAEDGTPIL (FL10) that is expressed in P. pentosaceus, a gram-positive lactic acid bacteria (LAB) that colonizes in the small intestine (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by hybridoma assay data in Figure 6e showing BEko8Z response to FL10 peptide.

claim: BEko8Z cells can recognize FL10 at concentrations as low as 1.5 nM.
source: While sensitivity to FL10 was ~1000 folds less than FL9 peptide, BEko8Z cells could recognize FL10 at concentrations as low as 1.5 nM.
evidence: Supported by dose-response data in Figure 6f showing BEko8Z response to varying concentrations of FL10.

claim: Sensitivity to FL10 is ~1000 folds less than FL9 peptide.
source: While sensitivity to FL10 was ~1000 folds less than FL9 peptide, BEko8Z cells could recognize FL10 at concentrations as low as 1.5 nM.
evidence: Supported by dose-response data in Figure 6f comparing BEko8Z responses to FL9 versus FL10.

claim: FYAEDDTPIV (FV10), an FL10 homologous peptide expressed in Lactobacillus johnsonii, fails to activate BEko8Z cells.
source: In contrast, FYAEDDTPIV(FV10), an FL10 homologous peptide expressed in Lactobacillus johnsonii which is a common LAB that colonizes the GI tract, failed to activate BEko8Z cells (Figure 6f, Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by hybridoma assay data in Figure 6f showing no BEko8Z response to FV10 peptide.

claim: Donor-derived QFLTg populations are present and phenotypically unaltered in the spleen and siIEL compartment of GF QFLTg_WT chimera mice at 8 weeks of age.
source: While the donor-derived QFLTg populations were present and phenotypically unaltered in the spleen and siIEL compartment of GF QFLTg_WT chimera mice at 8 weeks of age, they were barely detectable in the GF chimera mice at 16 weeks of age (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 showing presence and phenotype of donor QFLTg cells in 8 week GF chimera mice.

claim: Donor-derived QFLTg cells are barely detectable in GF chimera mice at 16 weeks of age.
source: While the donor-derived QFLTg populations were present and phenotypically unaltered in the spleen and siIEL compartment of GF QFLTg_WT chimera mice at 8 weeks of age, they were barely detectable in the GF chimera mice at 16 weeks of age (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 7b showing loss of donor QFLTg cells in 16 week GF chimera mice.

claim: Monocolonization of GF QFLTg_WT chimera mice with P. pentosaceus completely restores the donor-derived QFLTg population in both spleen and siIEL in 16 week GF chimera mice.
source: Notably, monocolonization of the GF QFLTg_WT chimera mice with P. pentosaceus completely restored the donor-derived QFLTg population in both tissues in 16 week GF chimera mice (Figure 7b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 7b showing restoration of donor QFLTg cells after P. pentosaceus colonization.

claim: Both P. pentosaceus and L. johnsonii efficiently colonize GF mice.
source: Analysis of the microbiome composition of fecal pallets showed that both species efficiently colonized the GF mice (Figure 7c).
evidence: Supported by metagenomic sequencing data in Figure 7c showing relative abundance of bacteria in colonized mice.

claim: The endogenous Vα3.2+QFL T population in the siIEL compartment is retained by P. pentosaceus colonization of GF mice at 16 weeks of age.
source: While the endogenous Vα3.2+QFL T population in the siIEL compartment was retained by P. pentosaceus colonization of GF mice at 16 weeks of age, L. johnsonii colonization failed to restore the population to a level comparable with SPF or P. pentosaceus colonized mice.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 7d showing maintenance of endogenous Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in P. pentosaceus colonized mice.

claim: L. johnsonii colonization fails to restore the endogenous Vα3.2+QFL T population in the siIEL compartment to a level comparable with SPF or P. pentosaceus colonized mice.
source: While the endogenous Vα3.2+QFL T population in the siIEL compartment was retained by P. pentosaceus colonization of GF mice at 16 weeks of age, L. johnsonii colonization failed to restore the population to a level comparable with SPF or P. pentosaceus colonized mice.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 7d showing lack of restoration of endogenous Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in L. johnsonii colonized mice.

claim: Maintenance of the endogenous splenic QFL T population is independent of microbes.
source: On the other hand, maintenance of the endogenous splenic QFL T population was independent of microbes, in line with our earlier observations (Figure 7d).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 7d showing no difference in splenic endogenous QFL T cells between colonized and uncolonized mice.

claim: Both donor-derived QFLTg cells and endogenous Vα3.2+QFL T cells from colonized GF chimera mice show a memory phenotype identical to that seen in SPF chimera mice.
source: Phenotype analysis revealed that both the donor-derived QFLTg cells and the endogenous Vα3.2+QFL T cells from the colonized GF chimera mice showed a memory phenotype identical to that seen in the SPF chimera mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3 comparing phenotypes in colonized GF versus SPF chimera mice.

claim: The late-life maintenance of Vα3.2+QFL T cells in the small intestine is dependent on the commensal bacterium P. pentosaceus which expresses a FL9 homolog peptide.
source: We thus conclude that the late-life maintenance of Vα3.2+QFL T cells in the small intestine was dependent on the commensal bacterium P. pentosaceus which expresses a FL9 homolog peptide.
evidence: Inferred from data showing restoration of QFL T cells by P. pentosaceus but not L. johnsonii colonization (Figure 7b, d), combined with identification of FL10 peptide in P. pentosaceus (Figure 6e).

claim: The unconventional phenotype of QFL T cells is likely acquired through microbe-independent mechanisms.
source: In addition, the unconventional phenotype of QFL T cells was likely acquired through microbe-independent mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from data showing similar phenotypes in young SPF and GF mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: The display of peptides by MHC class I molecules on the cell surface is critical for CD8+ T cell immune surveillance.
source: The display of peptides by MHC class I (MHC I) molecules on the cell surface is critical for CD8+ T cell immune surveillance (Shastri et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shastri et al., 2002.

claim: Loss of ERAP1 severely disrupts the peptide repertoire presented by both classical MHC Ia and nonclassical MHC Ib molecules.
source: Loss of ERAP1 severely disrupts the peptide repertoire presented by both the classical MHC Ia and the nonclassical MHC Ib molecules (Hammer et al., 2006; Hammer et al., 2007a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hammer et al., 2006 and Hammer et al., 2007a.

claim: Qa-1b presents a significantly increased number of peptides on the cell surface of ERAP1-KO cells compared with wild-type cells.
source: Qa-1b, a nonclassical MHC Ib molecule, has been shown to present a significantly increased number of peptides on the cell surface of ERAP1-KO cells as compared with wild-type (WT) cells (Nagarajan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nagarajan et al., 2016.

claim: FYAEATPML (FL9) peptide presented by Qa-1b was identified as an immunodominant ligand uniquely presented on ERAP1-deficient cells.
source: One peptide presented by Qa-1b, FYAEATPML (FL9) (with the Qa-1b-FL9 complex termed QFL), was identified as an immunodominant ligand uniquely presented on ERAP1-deficient cells (Nagarajan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nagarajan et al., 2012.

claim: QFL T cells are present at a frequency 10-fold higher in the spleen of naïve mice compared to conventional antigen-specific CD8+ T cells.
source: Unlike conventional antigen-specific CD8+ T cells which are typically detected at a frequency of 1 in 105~106, QFL T cells are present at a frequency 10-fold higher in the spleen of naïve mice with the bulk splenic QFL T population displaying a CD44hiCD122+ antigen-experienced phenotype (Nagarajan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nagarajan et al., 2012.

claim: A large proportion of the QFL T population expresses an invariant TCRα-chain Vα3.2Jα21.
source: T cell receptor (TCR) analysis of QFL T cells revealed that a large proportion of the QFL T population expresses an invariant TCRα-chain Vα3.2Jα21 (Guan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guan et al., 2017.

claim: CD8αα+ IELs were decreased in mice deficient for Qa-2.
source: For instance, while the loss of classical MHC Ia molecules showed little impact on the CD8αα+ IEL population, these cells were decreased in mice deficient for Qa-2 (Das et al., 2000; Das and Janeway, 1999; Park et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Das et al., 2000; Das and Janeway, 1999; Park et al., 1999.

claim: A population of CD8αα+ IEL precursors which preferentially expresses Vα3.2 was shown to be decreased in number in the absence of CD1d.
source: Furthermore, a population of CD8αα+ IEL precursors which preferentially expresses Vα3.2 was shown to be decreased in number in the absence of CD1d (Ruscher et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruscher et al., 2017.

claim: Studies of germ-free mice have shown extensive defects in gut-associated lymphoid tissues together with morphological changes in the intestine associated with the absence of gut microbiota.
source: Studies of germ-free (GF) mice have shown extensive defects in gut-associated lymphoid tissues together with morphological changes in the intestine associated with the absence of gut microbiota (Round and Mazmanian, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Round and Mazmanian, 2009.

claim: natIELs that do not rely on cognate antigens in the periphery are believed to home to the gut independent of microbes.
source: Notably, despite the critical role of gut microbiota in the establishment of the gut immune system, natIELs that do not rely on cognate antigens in the periphery are believed to be home to the gut independent of microbes (Mota-Santos et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mota-Santos et al., 1990.

claim: Unconventional T cells are typically characterized by recognition of ligands presented by non-classical MHC Ib, expression of invariant TCRs, residence in nonlymphoid tissues and innate-like functions.
source: These traits of QFL T cells indicate their potential similarity to other unconventional T cells, such as invariant NKT (iNKT) and mucosal-associated invariant T(MAIT) cells, which are typically characterized by recognition of ligands presented by non-classical MHC Ib, expression of invariant TCRs, residence in nonlymphoid tissues and innate-like functions (Godfrey et al., 2015; Salio et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Godfrey et al., 2015 and Salio et al., 2014.

claim: The small intestinal intraepithelial lymphocyte compartment is populated by unconventional T cells of both TCRɣδ+ and TCRαβ+ lineage which express CD8αα but lack CD4, CD8αβ, CD5, and CD90 expression.
source: The small intestinal intraepithelial lymphocyte (siIEL) compartment is populated by unconventional T cells of both TCRɣδ+ and TCRαβ+ lineage which express CD8αα but lack CD4, CD8αβ, CD5, and CD90 expression.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of IEL populations.

claim: CD8αα+CD4-CD8αβ-TCRαβ+ IELs are categorized as natural IELs (natIELs) because they acquire their activated phenotype in the thymus.
source: The development of the CD8αα+CD4-CD8αβ-TCRαβ+ population (CD8αα+ IEL), categorized as natural IELs (natIELs) because they acquire their activated phenotype in the thymus, has been extensively studied (Cheroutre et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheroutre et al., 2011.

claim: Cytokines including IL-15 and the combination of IL-7/IL-18 have been implicated in the maintenance and survival of both 'virtual' memory T cells and IELs.
source: Cytokines including IL-15 and the combination of IL-7/IL-18 have been implicated in the maintenance and survival of both 'virtual' memory T cells and IELs (Klose et al., 2014; Okazawa et al., 2004; Prasad et al., 2021; Schluns and Lefrançois, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klose et al., 2014; Okazawa et al., 2004; Prasad et al., 2021; Schluns and Lefrançois, 2003.

claim: The low IFN-ɣ production of IEL QFLTg cells is in keeping with their natIEL phenotype - antigen-experienced yet functionally quiescent.
source: The low IFN-ɣ production of IEL QFLTg cells was in keeping with their natIEL phenotype - antigen-experienced yet functionally quiescent (Cheroutre et al., 2011; Denning et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cheroutre et al., 2011 and Denning et al., 2007.

claim: Spontaneous IFN-ɣ secretion by IELs may be an important component of immunosurveillance at the mucosal surface, capable of identifying and eliminating transformed cells.
source: It has been proposed that spontaneous IFN-ɣ secretion by IELs may be an important component of immunosurveillance at the mucosal surface, capable of identifying and eliminating transformed cells (Carol et al., 1998; Reynisson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carol et al., 1998 and Reynisson et al., 2020.

claim: CD8αα+ IELs are intrinsically programmed for innate functionality, as shown by PMA/ionomycin-induced production of high levels of IFN-ɣ, CXCL2, etc.
source: CD8αα+ IELs are intrinsically programmed for innate functionality, as was shown by PMA/ionomycin-induced production of high levels of IFN-ɣ, CXCL2, etc. (Van Kaer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Van Kaer et al., 2014.

claim: Under physiological conditions, the activation of IELs is complex and highly regulated as TCRs and inhibitory coreceptors such as CD8αα are engaged.
source: However, our observation of the relative hyporesponsiveness of siIEL Vα3.2+QFL T to stimuli indicated that under physiological conditions, the activation of IELs was more complex and highly regulated as TCRs and inhibitory coreceptors such as CD8αα were engaged (Cheroutre and Lambolez, 2008; Macpherson and Harris, 2004).
evidence: Inferred from data showing hyporesponsiveness of siIEL QFLTg cells, supported by citations to Cheroutre and Lambolez, 2008 and Macpherson and Harris, 2004.

claim: The gut QFL T cells are constantly challenged by microbial or dietary antigens from the gut lumen.
source: It is not surprising that the gut QFL T cells were functionally quiescent as these cells are constantly challenged by the microbial or dietary antigens from the gut lumen (Denning et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Denning et al., 2007 and general knowledge of gut environment.

claim: Vα3.2-expressing QFL T cells represent an unconventional population of Qa-1b-restricted CD8+ T cells which naturally reside at high frequency in small intestine epithelium.
source: In conclusion, Vα3.2-expressing QFL T cells represent an unconventional population of Qa-1b-restricted CD8+ T cells which naturally reside at high frequency in small intestine epithelium.
evidence: Summarizes findings from multiple experiments showing high frequency of Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in siIEL and their Qa-1b dependence.

claim: Vα3.2+QFL T cells have memory phenotypes in the spleen and reveal the characteristics of natIELs in the gut.
source: These cells have memory phenotypes in the spleen and reveal the characteristics of natIELs in the gut.
evidence: Summarizes findings showing CD44hi phenotype in spleen and CD8αα+ phenotype in gut.

claim: Vα3.2+QFL T cells cross-react with FL9 homolog peptide expressed in a commensal bacterium.
source: In addition, the fact that Vα3.2+QFL T cross-reacts with FL9 homolog peptide expressed in a commensal bacterium suggests that these cells might be functionally versatile.
evidence: Supported by data showing BEko8Z response to FL10 peptide from P. pentosaceus (Figure 6e, f).

claim: Vα3.2+QFL T cells might be functionally versatile.
source: In addition, the fact that Vα3.2+QFL T cross-reacts with FL9 homolog peptide expressed in a commensal bacterium suggests that these cells might be functionally versatile.
evidence: Speculated based on cross-reactivity with bacterial peptide.

claim: Splenic Vα3.2+QFL T cells display a memory phenotype and acquire this phenotype in a Qa-1b dependent manner.
source: Here, we found that splenic Vα3.2+QFL T cells display a memory phenotype and the corresponding rapid effector function, but acquire this phenotype in a Qa-1b dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by data showing loss of CD44hi phenotype in Qa-1b-KO mice (Figure 3b, c).

claim: QFL T cells might be exposed to transiently induced QFL epitope on cells due to various intracellular stressors that might affect ERAP1 function.
source: Given the unique dependence on Qa-1b expression for the phenotype imprinting of QFL T cells, it is possible that QFL T cells are exposed to transiently induced QFL epitope on cells due to various intracellular stressors that might affect ERAP1 function.
evidence: Speculated as a possible mechanism for Qa-1b-dependent phenotype imprinting.

claim: QFL T cells might cross-react with Qa-1b presented FL9 homolog peptide(s).
source: Alternatively, QFL T cells might cross-react with Qa-1b presented FL9 homolog peptide(s).
evidence: Speculated as an alternative mechanism, later supported by identification of FL10 peptide.

claim: The Qa-1b-FL10 ligand itself is unlikely to be directly associated with the memory imprinting for QFL T cells as these cells showed unaltered phenotypes in germ-free mice.
source: However, the Qa-1b-FL10 ligand itself is unlikely to be directly associated with the memory imprinting for QFL T cells as these cells showed unaltered phenotypes in germ-free mice.
evidence: Inferred from data showing similar phenotypes in young SPF and GF mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: There might be other unidentified self-peptide(s) presented by Qa-1b that are involved in memory phenotype imprinting of QFL T cells.
source: There might be other unidentified self-peptide(s) presented by Qa-1b that are involved in the process.
evidence: Speculated as a possible mechanism for Qa-1b-dependent phenotype imprinting.

claim: There may be some level of degeneracy in the TCR-Qa-1b interaction, so the precise peptide being presented is less critical than the presence of any peptide-Qa-1b complex.
source: It is also possible that there is some level of degeneracy in the TCR-Qa-1b interaction, so the precise peptide being presented is less critical than the presence of any peptide-Qa-1b complex.
evidence: Speculated as an alternative explanation for Qa-1b-dependent phenotype.

claim: The FL9 peptide binds to Qa-1b in a manner potentially similar to Qdm.
source: It is worth noting that the predicted structure of QFL-TCR:FL9:Qa-1b complex indicated that the FL9 peptide binds to Qa-1b in a manner potentially similar to Qdm.
evidence: Based on AlphaFold2 structure prediction and comparison with Qdm:Qa-1b crystal structure.

claim: The binding groove of Qa-1b and its human homolog HLA-E display remarkable structural homology.
source: Because the binding groove of Qa-1b and its human homolog HLA-E display remarkable structural homology (Zeng et al., 2012), it is possible that HLA-E can present FL9 or its homolog peptides and further support the establishment of a QFL T-like CD8 T population.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeng et al., 2012.

claim: HLA-E can possibly present FL9 or its homolog peptides and support the establishment of a QFL T-like CD8 T population.
source: Because the binding groove of Qa-1b and its human homolog HLA-E display remarkable structural homology (Zeng et al., 2012), it is possible that HLA-E can present FL9 or its homolog peptides and further support the establishment of a QFL T-like CD8 T population.
evidence: Speculated based on structural homology between Qa-1b and HLA-E.

claim: HLA-E-restricted CD8 T cells can recognize a broad repertoire of peptides presented upon vaccination and provide protection against HIV-1 infection.
source: Studies on cytomegalovirus-vectored vaccines have shown that HLA-E-restricted CD8 T cells could recognize a broad repertoire of peptides presented upon vaccination and provide protection against HIV-1 infection (Hansen et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hansen et al., 2016 and Yang et al., 2021.

claim: The Vα3.2-expressing CD8αβ+ T population is comprised of a relatively larger proportion of memory phenotype cells in the spleen than the non-Vα3.2 expressing population.
source: In line with a previous study, we observed that the Vα3.2-expressing CD8αβ+ T population was comprised of a relatively larger proportion of memory phenotype cells in the spleen than the non-Vα3.2 expressing population (Prasad et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and citation to Prasad et al., 2021.

claim: Memory phenotype non-QFL Vα3.2+CD8αβ+ T cells are lost in Qa-1b-KO mice.
source: In addition, these memory phenotype non-QFL Vα3.2+CD8αβ+ T cells were lost in Qa-1b-KO mice.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c showing loss of CD44hi cells in Vα3.2+ population in Qa-1b-KO mice.

claim: Vα3.2+QFL T cells are likely only one prototypical example of Qa-1b restricted Vα3.2+CD8+ T cell clones with memory phenotype and innate-like function.
source: These results indicate that Vα3.2+QFL T cells are likely only one prototypical example of Qa-1b restricted Vα3.2+CD8+ T cell clones with memory phenotype and innate-like function.
evidence: Inferred from observations that total Vα3.2+ CD8+ T cells show similar Qa-1b-dependent memory phenotype.

claim: Abundant Vα3.2+QFL T cells are detected in small intestine epithelium which show the signature phenotype of natIELs including expression of CD8αα and lack of CD4, CD8αβ, CD5, and CD90.
source: We detected abundant Vα3.2+QFL T cells in small intestine epithelium which showed the signature phenotype of natIELs including expression of CD8αα and lack of CD4, CD8αβ, CD5, and CD90.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2c, d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAP is required for the presence of gut Vα3.2+QFL T cells.
source: Similar to the splenic population, while TAP is required for the presence of the population, the unconventional phenotype of Vα3.2+QFL T cells in the gut is strongly Qa-1b-dependent.
evidence: Supported by data showing absence of siIEL Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in TAP-KO mice (Figure 3a).

claim: The unconventional phenotype of Vα3.2+QFL T cells in the gut is strongly Qa-1b-dependent.
source: Similar to the splenic population, while TAP is required for the presence of the population, the unconventional phenotype of Vα3.2+QFL T cells in the gut is strongly Qa-1b-dependent.
evidence: Supported by data showing loss of CD8αα+ phenotype in Qa-1b-KO mice (Figure 3d, e).

claim: QFL T cells are likely a distinct population which undergoes alternative developmental stages requiring TAP-dependent presentation of FL9 for positive selection and Qa-1b for acquiring their unconventional features.
source: It is worth noting that compared with the other Qa-1b-restrict T cells reported, such as a population of semi-invariant T cells which recognize TAP-independent peptides (Doorduijn et al., 2018) or an insulin peptide-specific CD8 T population (Sullivan et al., 2002), QFL T is likely a distinct population which undergoes alternative developmental stages which requires TAP-dependent presentation of FL9 (Nagarajan et al., 2012) (or other alternative essential peptides) for positive selection and Qa-1b for acquiring their unconventional features.
evidence: Inferred from data showing TAP requirement for presence and Qa-1b requirement for phenotype, with citations to Doorduijn et al., 2018; Sullivan et al., 2002; Nagarajan et al., 2012.

claim: CD8αα+ IELs can be restricted to KbDb, CD1d, or even unknown MHC Ib molecules.
source: Additionally, it is so far reported that CD8αα+ IELs can be restricted to KbDb, CD1d, or even unknown MHC Ib molecules (Mayans et al., 2014; Ruscher et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mayans et al., 2014 and Ruscher et al., 2017.

claim: Abundant Qa-1b-restricted TCRαβ+ natIELs are present in the gut.
source: Here by characterization of the gut Vα3.2+QFL T cells, we showed evidence of abundant Qa-1b-restricted TCRαβ+ natIELs being present in the gut.
evidence: Inferred from data showing Vα3.2+ QFL T cells in gut with natIEL phenotype and Qa-1b dependence.

claim: siIEL Vα3.2+QFL T cells display higher basal levels of intracellular IFN-ɣ than CD8αβ+ IELs.
source: Notably, although the siIEL Vα3.2+QFL T cells showed delayed and reduced IFN-ɣ production in response to the cognate peptide, they displayed higher basal levels of intracellular IFN-ɣ than CD8αβ+ IELs.
evidence: Supported by intracellular cytokine staining data in Figure 4i, j.

claim: siIEL QFL T cells may be poised for immediate elimination of abnormal cells.
source: Thus, siIEL QFL T cells may likewise be poised for immediate elimination of abnormal cells.
evidence: Speculated based on higher basal IFN-ɣ levels and cited role of IFN-ɣ in immunosurveillance.

claim: Under physiological conditions, the activation of IELs is complex and highly regulated as TCRs and inhibitory coreceptors such as CD8αα are engaged.
source: However, our observation of the relative hyporesponsiveness of siIEL Vα3.2+QFL T to stimuli indicated that under physiological conditions, the activation of IELs was more complex and highly regulated as TCRs and inhibitory coreceptors such as CD8αα were engaged (Cheroutre and Lambolez, 2008; Macpherson and Harris, 2004).
evidence: Inferred from hyporesponsiveness data and supported by citations to Cheroutre and Lambolez, 2008 and Macpherson and Harris, 2004.

claim: The presence of other possible signals generated from colonization of the commensal bacterium, such as secretion of bacteriocins, cannot be excluded.
source: Despite the evidence, we remain cautious of other possible signals generated from colonization of the commensal bacterium, such as secretion of bacteriocins.
evidence: Acknowledged as a limitation and alternative explanation.
